profiles.meeting_scenario: At a university hospital craniofacial center, an oral and maxillofacial surgeon and the lead biomedical imaging specialist are holding a planning meeting to prepare the center's first fully three-dimensional computerized orthognathic surgical planning workflow for a block of upcoming bimaxillary cases. The context is that the department wants to phase out its usual two-dimensional cephalometric tracing and plaster model surgery for selected patients over the next quarter, while still fitting the new workflow into existing clinic, radiology, and OR schedules. The agenda is to agree on what the '3D plan' package will include for each case, how imaging and dental data will be acquired and merged, who will own each step from scan acquisition to surgical splint/guide preparation, and what timeline should be used before the pre-op conference. The expected outcome is a seemingly shared implementation plan for the pilot workflow, including responsibilities, turnaround expectations, and what materials will be ready for the surgeon's case review.

members.name: Dr. Elena Vargas
members.expertise: Orthognathic surgery, dentofacial deformity correction, operative sequencing, preoperative case review
members.background: Associate professor at the hospital's craniofacial service who has planned complex bimaxillary and asymmetry cases for over a decade using 2D cephalometrics, facebow-mounted casts, and conventional model surgery; she is enthusiastic about digital planning but expects it to support existing surgical decision making rather than restructure the clinical pathway.
members.private_state: She wants the digital pilot to look smooth and clinically dependable with minimal extra clinic burden, and she is especially concerned about avoiding delays to already-booked OR dates or having to personally troubleshoot technical data problems close to surgery.
hidden_assumptions: A '3D plan' is a surgeon-facing operative planning packet centered on final jaw movements and splint-ready outputs, not a broader engineering dataset.
If a patient already has a diagnostic CBCT from orthodontic workup, that scan is usually sufficient for planning unless there is an obvious artifact issue.

When the team says the plan is 'ready for conference,' it means all clinically actionable components are finalized enough to present to anesthesia and OR schedulers, not merely that a draft simulation exists.
Dental surface detail will be incorporated through the same intraoral scan files the orthodontist routinely sends, with no special extra acquisition session.
The imaging specialist will handle data cleanup and registration as part of normal digital planning support without needing explicit delegation.

members.name: Alex Chen
members.expertise: Craniofacial image segmentation, CBCT/CT processing, multimodal registration, virtual surgical planning workflow design
members.background: Master's-trained bioengineer who recently joined from a medical device lab where he built semi-automated workflows for craniofacial modeling and 3D printed guides; he has strong technical confidence in volumetric planning pipelines but limited exposure to the informal conventions of a busy surgical service.
members.private_state: He wants to establish a reproducible, technically rigorous workflow that showcases the value of digital planning and avoids downstream rework caused by poor source data, and he is worried that the clinic may treat the software as a quick visualization tool instead of a data-dependent process.
hidden_assumptions: A '3D plan' includes a validated composite model with segmented skeleton, registered dentition, landmark set, and simulation files, even if splint fabrication is decided later.
For a pilot workflow, planning-quality imaging means a standardized recent scan acquired under the department's protocol rather than whatever outside or prior CBCT happens to be available.

When the plan is 'ready for conference,' it means the simulation has reached an internal technical review state where major movements can be discussed, not that manufacturing files and final approvals are complete.

Dental registration for orthognathic planning requires a dedicated high-resolution optical dentition capture or scanned casts obtained specifically for this workflow, because routine orthodontic files are often incomplete for occlusal accuracy.
The surgical service will explicitly indicate which cases need splints or printed models after the digital simulation is reviewed, since fabrication is a separate downstream step.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly refer to delivering 'the 3D plan' for each orthognathic case.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Vargas means a clinically final package: approved jaw movements, occlusion checked, and outputs far enough along that splint production can proceed without another planning pass.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Alex means a technically complete virtual planning dataset and simulation suitable for surgeon review, which may still precede fabrication decisions and final clinical sign-off.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In real planning meetings, '3D plan' sounds like an obvious shared term and both parties are genuinely discussing the same cases and software workflow, so neither notices that one is using it as a review milestone and the other as a near-final deliverable.

misalignment_points.topic: Which scan is being used as the pre-op image
misalignment_points.surface_form: They talk about using 'the pre-op CBCT' already in the chart for the pilot cases.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Vargas is thinking of the existing diagnostic CBCT obtained 4-6 months earlier during orthodontic workup, which she views as the standing pre-op image unless a new problem has arisen.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Alex is thinking of a new department-protocol CBCT acquired within a short window before planning, because that is what he considers the pre-op scan for a reproducible 3D workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both hospital staff commonly say 'the pre-op CBCT' as if there is only one relevant scan, and because many patients do have a prior diagnostic volume in the chart, each participant assumes the other is referring to the same imaging instance.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that each case should be 'ready for conference' by the Thursday pre-op review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Vargas believes this means the case is fully settled from a clinical planning standpoint, with movement values and practical downstream products effectively locked so the conference can serve as a final endorsement.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Alex believes this means a technically reviewed simulation is prepared for discussion, with the conference itself serving to finalize movements and determine whether fabrication should proceed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds operational rather than conceptual; both think they are simply aligning to the same deadline, but they silently attach different completion thresholds to that milestone.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in 'getting the dental scan'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Alex will 'get the dental scan merged in' before planning.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Vargas assumes this includes obtaining whatever orthodontic intraoral files already exist, cleaning them if needed, and integrating them without additional patient appointments.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Alex assumes his role starts once a dedicated planning-quality dentition scan or cast scan has been formally ordered and captured; he does not include arranging a new acquisition or salvaging ad hoc orthodontic files within 'merge it in.'
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see dental data integration as a routine support task beneath the level of explicit negotiation, and the phrase 'get the dental scan merged in' compresses acquisition, file retrieval, quality control, and registration into a single apparently obvious step.

turns.inner_thought: We need this to feel like a clean upgrade from the usual model surgery packet, not a science project. For these next few bimax cases, the 3D plan should function as the operative planning package I can rely on, with the jaw movements settled and the case far enough along that splints can move forward without another whole round of work. I do not want extra clinic friction or technical loose ends landing on my desk right before an OR date.
turns.utterance: What I'd like today is a workable rollout for the next few bimaxillary cases so we can start using the 3D plan in place of the usual model surgery packet. If we can keep it practical and fit it into the current flow, I think we can get the pilot off the ground without too much disruption.

turns.inner_thought: Good, this is a chance to establish a proper end-to-end digital workflow. The 3D plan, to me, starts with a planning-quality pre-op CBCT under a consistent protocol, then segmentation, dentition registration, landmarks, simulation, and internal review. If we define ready for conference as the point when the simulation is technically complete enough for discussion, we can avoid rushing fabrication decisions before the anatomy and alignment are validated.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can support that. I'd suggest we keep a standard pipeline for the pilot cases: start from the pre-op CBCT, move through segmentation and registration, build the simulation, and then have each case ready for conference for review.

turns.inner_thought: Most of these patients already have a diagnostic CBCT sitting in the chart from orthodontic workup, and that should be enough unless there's some obvious artifact. I really do not want to create a new radiology visit just to satisfy the pilot; that will slow everything down and irritate patients and staff.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Most of the pilot patients already have a pre-op CBCT in the chart from the orthodontic workup, so I'd like us to use those where we can and avoid bringing people back for an extra visit.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the pre-op CBCT is in the system in the format I need, I can proceed. And once the dental data for this workflow has been captured and provided, getting the dental scan merged in is straightforward on my side. I am assuming someone upstream will make sure the proper dentition scan or cast scan exists; my task is the registration and composite model build, not chasing ad hoc orthodontic files.
turns.utterance: In principle, yes. Once the scan is in the system, I can get the dental scan merged in and build out the composite model for each case, so from there the planning steps should be pretty consistent.

If this works, the digital packet should come together behind the scenes much like our current support processes do.
turns.utterance: That's ideal, because the orthodontists usually already have the intraoral files. I'd really like the 3D plan assembled without creating another appointment for the patient if we can help it.

turns.inner_thought: I need a predictable milestone. If Thursday means ready for conference in the technical sense, I can have the segmentation, registration, landmarks, and simulation reviewed on my side so the surgeons can make decisions consistently. The conference should be where major movements are confirmed and any downstream manufacturing is triggered, not where everyone assumes the whole package is already locked.
turns.utterance: My goal would be to have each case ready for conference by Thursday. That gives us a regular point in the week to review the movements consistently before anything proceeds downstream.

turns.inner_thought: Thursday is exactly when I need the case essentially buttoned up. If it's ready for conference, I want to walk out knowing the plan is settled enough for anesthesia, scheduling, and the operative timeline, not still open-ended. The whole point is to avoid last-minute uncertainty.
turns.utterance: Thursday works well for me. Once a case is ready for conference, I'd want to be able to leave that review with something essentially set for the operative timeline.

turns.inner_thought: I should spell out the core deliverables as I see them without getting into fabrication yet. The 3D plan package for the pilot is the validated virtual planning dataset: segmented anatomy, registered dentition, landmarks, and the simulation files. That's the foundation. Splints or printed models can be decided after surgeon review once the movements are confirmed.
turns.utterance: For the pilot cases, the core 3D plan package I'd prepare would be the segmented anatomy, the registered dentition, the landmark set, and the simulation files. That should give us a consistent base across the first group of cases.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine, but for the first two patients especially, I need the 3D plan to behave like a near-final operative packet. I cannot have those cases reviewed on Thursday and then discover we're still one or two process steps away from splint prep. The whole value here is eliminating the last-minute scramble.
turns.utterance: Good. And for the first two patients in particular, I'd like the 3D plan to flow directly into splint preparation so we don't create a last-minute scramble.
